EDF.MAIN_TITLE: Availability of the French nuclear fleet (Present, past and forecast)
EDF.NAV_MAP: Map of French nuclear fleet availability
EDF.INFO_TEXT: This map displays the availability of the nuclear fleet at a specific date and time. By default, it shows today's date and current time (Europe/Paris timezone). To view past or forecast fleet availability, select a date/time pair using the filters on the left. Units with 0 MW available power are displayed in orange; otherwise they are displayed in green. The geographical positioning of nuclear units has been adjusted for better readability on the map of France.

ABSTRACT.TITLE: Abstract
ABSTRACT.CONTENT: These data show the current, past and forecast availability of the French nuclear fleet over a rolling year. You will find, plant by plant, and for each unit, their available power in MW. This data is updated at the beginning of each hour.

HERO.TITLE: How does nuclear energy work?
HERO.SUBTITLE: From uranium fuel to your power outlet, understand everything in a few minutes.

FISSION.TITLE: Nuclear fission: the spark behind it all
FISSION.LEAD: A nuclear power plant works like a giant kettle. But instead of a gas burner, it uses the heat released by uranium fission.
FISSION.TEXT: Fission is the splitting of a heavy atom (uranium-235) into two smaller atoms, triggered by a neutron impact. This reaction releases a colossal amount of energy as heat, along with 2 to 3 new neutrons that in turn trigger more fissions — this is the chain reaction.
FISSION.INFO_BOX: By the numbers: 1 kg of fissioned uranium releases as much energy as burning 2,700 tonnes of coal.

FONCTIONNEMENT.TITLE: How a nuclear power plant works
FONCTIONNEMENT.SUBTITLE: French plants are Pressurized Water Reactors (PWR). Here is how they convert heat into electricity, step by step.
FONCTIONNEMENT.STEP1_DESC: Assemblies of enriched uranium rods form the reactor core.
FONCTIONNEMENT.STEP2_DESC: Fission heats the water in the primary circuit to ~320°C at 155 bars. The water stays liquid.
FONCTIONNEMENT.STEP3_DESC: The heat is transferred to a secondary circuit (non-radioactive) which turns into steam.
FONCTIONNEMENT.STEP4_DESC: The steam spins a turbine at high speed — heat → mechanical energy.
FONCTIONNEMENT.STEP5_DESC: The turbine drives an alternator — mechanical energy → electricity.
FONCTIONNEMENT.STEP6_DESC: The voltage is raised to 400,000 V for long-distance transmission with minimal losses.
FONCTIONNEMENT.COOLING: What about the cooling towers? The steam that drove the turbine is cooled in a condenser. The white vapour visible above the towers is not smoke — it is purified water vapour, completely harmless.

CIRCUITS.TITLE: The 3 circuits of a PWR plant
CIRCUITS.SUBTITLE: Three separate and sealed water loops ensure that no radioactivity ever leaves the reactor.
CIRCUITS.C1_DESC: Pressurized water in direct contact with the reactor core. Sealed inside a reinforced-concrete containment building 1.2 m thick. Never leaves the reactor building.
CIRCUITS.C2_DESC: Receives heat via a heat exchanger. Turns to steam and drives the turbine. The water is then cooled and recycled in a closed loop.
CIRCUITS.C3_DESC: Cools the steam from circuit 2 to condense it back to water. Can use river water, seawater, or cooling towers.

RESEAU.TITLE: From the plant to your socket
RESEAU.SUBTITLE: The electricity produced travels thousands of kilometres and undergoes several voltage transformations before reaching you.
RESEAU.INFO_BOX: Why step up to 400,000 V? The higher the voltage, the lower the losses in the cables. Transmitting electricity at very high voltage divides losses by thousands over long distances — essential for connecting plants to distant cities.

CHIFFRES.SUBTITLE: France is the most nuclear-dependent country in the world for its electricity supply.
